research_tasks: Research log (2026-10-11, first run, mode create, empty baseline). Opened 33 sources and failed to open 2 (S34, S35). Read in full: the Rolling Stone feature (S01), the Vanity Fair profile (S02), The Line of Best Fit, Billboard, SongwriterUniverse and Elite Daily interviews (S03-S06), and caption transcripts of nine video interviews dated March 27 to August 19, 2026 (S07-S15, about 23,000 words). Read the controversy coverage, two album reviews, The New Yorker essay and the trade reports through October 6, 2026. Evidence was gathered before a type was chosen. Outcome: no defensible discriminator; subject meets open-case eligibility (adult, breakout in January to March 2026, the entire interview record is one seven-month promotional cycle). Status ready, profile_format open_case, leading read Type 9 at low confidence, Type 7 as the alternative, Types 6 and 3 live. Risks set: contested_typing (required) and sensitive_allegations (plagiarism and bought-career allegations, C13 and C14), so the six-role jury applies.

Accuracy check (2026-10-11). Latest developments found: Billboard's September 27 report that she left Disruptor Management (C18); the October 1 cut-for-time SNL sketch and her response (C16); the October 6 report that Shaylen and TAELA allege her unreleased song 'Badly' copies 'WATCH THIS', with no response from her (C13). No statement from her on the song-similarity allegations was found. Grammy nominations are due November 16, 2026 (C31). open_case.next_review is set to 2026-12-01, after those nominations and the announced end of her first headline tour on November 23, 2026.

Drafting guidance (open case). Follow the standard's 'Open case profiles' section: open with who she is and why people are searching (No. 2 Hot 100 single, debut album, backlash), then name the open question. Show what the record does show, dated and sourced, with limits. Set Type 9 beside Types 7, 6 and 3 with the best evidence for and against each. Include an H2 beginning '## What would settle it' built from open_case.settle_signals. Keep '## What is Stella Lefty's personality type?' with an answer of at most 60 words in 'leading read, held loosely' language. Target 1,200 to 2,500 words. Titles, description and FAQs must say 'leading read' or 'open case', never 'is a Type 9'. Set enneagram: 9 and published: false.

Allegations rule (from the queue entry and the standard). Plagiarism and bought-career claims are allegations: attribute each to its accuser with a date, state which comparisons carry credits (Kahan; Sillers and Selby) and which do not, note that no legal claim or finding has been reported, and never use them as evidence of character or type. Do not adopt Paste's 'impending lawsuit' wording (S33) or the nickname coined by her critics in the article's own voice.

Quotation cautions. S07-S15 are caption transcripts without speaker labels: check each printed quote against the video's audio and timestamp. Do not quote as hers: 'It lowers my cortisol' (S07, about 06:10), 'With one person... do you hate me?' (S13, about 03:33) or 'Why change... If you loved it at 15' (S15, about 07:37) unless audio confirms the speaker. 'Addicted to the virality' is the host's paraphrase (S07). The Variety quote reproduced in S31 has no opened original. Vanity Fair's 'preventing any risk of legal action' is the writer's phrase, not hers.

Sensitivity. Her mother's cancer and her friend's death (C25) are single-source and concern other people's health: use only as her stated reason for studying public health, with no causal personality claim, no name for the friend and no update on her mother. Do not print a net-worth figure without a dated attribution (C02). Use the full birth date only as supported in C01.

sources.title: Stella Lefty Was Covering Noah Kahan on TikTok. Now She Has One of the Year's Biggest Songs
sources.speaker: Stella Lefty, interviewed in person by Marissa R. Moss (Rolling Stone); also quotes Adam Alpert, Wyatt Flores and Dan Smyers
sources.locator: Feature body. CMA Fest scene (opening four paragraphs); 'I love to post' paragraph; mother's diagnosis and best friend's death paragraphs; publishing-deal paragraph ('You seem more like an artist'); Alpert quote ('I don't even want feedback'); 'unnatural' / 'Double-edged sword' paragraph; closing paragraph ('go home and write more songs').
sources.excerpt: “They said to me, ‘You seem more like an artist,’ which really pissed me off at the time because I was like, a bunch of dudes don’t get to tell me what to do,” [...] “It’s just so unnatural to see so many people having opinions about me,” [...] “At the end of the day, I just focus on the people that do. This is what I decided to do. Double-edged sword.”
sources.context: The only long in-person feature so far. Reported at CMA Fest in Nashville in June 2026, with her parents and boyfriend present. The reporter's own observation: 'Everyone seems a little panicked that we won't make it where we need to go in time, except for Lefty herself.' Source for her mother's cancer diagnosis when she was 13 and her high-school best friend's death (her account, partly paraphrased by the writer). Alpert was her manager at the time and is an interested party; Flores and Smyers are performers she has shared stages with.

claims.claim: Stella Lefty was born Stella Lefkofsky on August 13, 2002, and grew up in Chicago's North Shore suburbs. Her age is tracked separately in C114.
claims.passage: Lefty was born Stella Lefkofsky on August 13, 2002
claims.inference: She gives the day and month herself ('my birthday's August 13th', S14) and confirms the year when a host asks 'you were born 2002?' (S07). The body links 'the day' to S14 and 'the year' to S07. Glencoe, two brothers and New Trier are from Vanity Fair (S02) and Elite Daily (S06). The body no longer prints a present-tense age.
claims.alternative: She describes home as the 'Winnetka area' on Chicago radio (S14); Glencoe and Winnetka adjoin, so write 'North Shore suburbs' or 'Glencoe' but do not present them as a contradiction. Ages printed in 2026 coverage (23 before August 13, 24 after) are consistent with the date.

claims.claim: Her father is Eric Lefkofsky, who co-founded Groupon and founded Tempus AI. The article prints no net-worth figure and no current job title.
claims.passage: Her father, Eric Lefkofsky, co-founded Groupon and founded Tempus AI
claims.inference: Billboard (S04) calls him 'Groupon co-founder and Tempus AI founder/CEO'. Edit stage: the body and the father FAQ now give only the two founding facts, which do not expire, so the chief-executive title and any net-worth figure are out of the article.
claims.alternative: Paste suggests the stage name puts distance between her and her father (S25); her account and the brothers' use of the name cut against that, but the name does make the connection less visible. Prefer 'billionaire' with a dated Forbes attribution over a precise number.

claims.claim: Career sequence as the article states it: she moved to Los Angeles in September 2024, released the pop EP Tragic, Really in 2025, decided in December 2025 to return to country-leaning songs, and released 'Boston' on March 27, 2026.
claims.passage: In September 2024 she moved to Los Angeles
claims.inference: Each step is dated by at least one opened interview or profile: 'her 2024 debut single' (S01); Los Angeles in September 2024 and the March 27 release (S06); January singles and the Atlantic Outpost signing (S04); the May 15 EP (S04, S05); the August 21 album (S02). Wikipedia supplies the July 15, 2025 EP date (S28).
claims.alternative: Sources disagree on small points: when she began posting (2020 in S09 and S12, 2021 in S02 and S05, 2022 for singing in S01), and one explainer misdates 'Boston' to February 2026. Say 'since about 2020' for posting and use March 27, 2026 for 'Boston'.

claims.claim: As of Billboard's report of September 27, 2026, 'Boston' had peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100.
claims.passage: it had peaked at No. 2 on the Hot 100
claims.inference: Billboard's own September 27 report (S17): 'The song also peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100.' Edit stage: the Country Airplay and Billboard 200 figures were cut, because the same report describes the Country Airplay run as ongoing ('for a second consecutive week').
claims.alternative: These are peaks at a date and can change. The VMA outcome was not confirmed in an opened primary source. Nothing here bears on personality; it explains why readers are searching.
claims.review_trigger: Recheck the Hot 100 peak before each publish or refresh; it is a peak as of a dated report.

claims.claim: She describes being 'terrified' of singing in front of anybody when she was younger, and says one listener is harder for her than thousands (C48).
claims.passage: "I just was so afraid of singing in front of anybody. Terrified. My worst nightmare when I was younger,"
claims.inference: Repeated in four interviews across five months and two countries, with consistent detail, so it is at least a stable part of how she understands herself. It suggests the fear attaches to being judged at close range by a person in the room, which a phone camera avoided. That reading is an inference; she says only that small audiences are scarier (S13).
claims.alternative: Performance anxiety is common among performers and is a likeable origin-story beat that interviewers keep requesting. Her mother remembers a child who had to be told to keep the singing down at home (S01), and Rolling Stone reports in-person gigs as a duo in her college years (C93), so the fear did not keep her from audiences. Not type-diagnostic alone.

claims.claim: She says that at Tulane she learned professional songwriters exist and set out to write for other artists, not to perform.
claims.passage: "I wanted to write for other people."
claims.inference: Told the same way in at least five interviews. The article quotes The Line of Best Fit ('When I figured out what a songwriter was my junior year, I became set on being a songwriter. I wanted to write for other people.') and now words it as the career she 'says she wanted'. Edit stage: 'hidden' and 'unseen' are gone from the body, the FAQs and the closing paragraph.
claims.alternative: A retrospective account given after stardom, and one that suits the 'accidental star' answer to the industry-plant charge. Rolling Stone records in-person gigs as Stella + Huck and a viral original in the same years (C93), and that she had dreamed of being an artist (S01), so wanting to be heard predates the songwriter plan.

claims.claim: In 2024, about a week after graduating, a Nashville music publisher she had been writing for told her she seemed like an artist; by her account she was angry at being told what she was, and within months concluded they were right.
claims.passage: "You don't get to tell me what I am."
claims.inference: Her quoted reaction is consistent across two interviews ('You don't get to tell me what I am', S03; 'a bunch of dudes don't get to tell me what to do', S01), as is the later agreement. Edit stage: the article no longer counts this as an instance of going along. It is presented as the mirror image of the pattern (resist first, agree later) and as counterevidence to a conflict-shy reading, with the note that 'I was like' may report a thought.
claims.alternative: The three opened accounts differ on who ended the deal (C38, C87, C88). Anger at being redefined by strangers is ordinary and not type-specific. Nothing shows she said it aloud.

claims.claim: She says she loves to post and could do it '700 times a day', and that she kept writing songs about boys her friends knew over their objections.
claims.passage: "I could do it 700 times a day. People were like, 'Chill.'"
claims.inference: Rolling Stone gives the volume ('I could do it 700 times a day', S01); Virgin Radio gives the friends' objection and her reply (S09, C51).
claims.alternative: She also frames posting as a generational default (S09) and as pandemic-era behavior everyone shared (S12). Her posts from before August 2025 are no longer public (C81), so none of this can be checked against the videos. Persisting despite friends' objections cuts against a conflict-avoidant reading.

claims.claim: In her early posting she wanted to sing whatever cover was going viral at the time.
claims.passage: she wanted to sing whatever cover was "going viral at the time."
claims.inference: Caption and second transcription agree on 'going viral at the time' (S07). The article uses it in the paragraph on watching what worked and lists it under Type 3.
claims.alternative: 'Addicted to the virality' is the interviewer's paraphrase and is not used. Vanity Fair reports that she and her co-writers say they do not think about the algorithm while writing (C94).

claims.claim: Her accounts of the Los Angeles pop year vary. In March 2026 she says she 'pivoted for a whole year' and names no adviser (C85). From May she says people told her to avoid country because she was not from the South, 'and it really got in my head'. In August she says she thought success required a distinct brand (C86).
claims.passage: "I had so many people telling me what to make and it really got in my head, so I went for more of a pop-alternative direction because that's what they all wanted me to do."
claims.inference: Direct quotation from SongwriterUniverse, May 15, 2026 (S05); 'because I wasn't from the South' is from the sentence immediately before in the same answer. Edit stage correction: the earlier statement that she tells this 'the same way in five interviews' was wrong. A reread of S13 and S07 shows three different accounts, and the article now sets them out by date. The adviser version is the one that has the comply-then-reverse shape the leading read rests on.
claims.alternative: The earliest telling (S13) has her pivoting on her own and afraid; the May answer begins 'Yes, I was definitely exploring different sounds'. A 22-year-old following newly signed managers is ordinary. The story ends where audience response was strongest (C90), and attributing a disappointing year to other people's advice is the main rival to 'she goes along' (C105).

claims.claim: Her then-manager Adam Alpert told Rolling Stone that she came to his team saying she had found what she was looking for and knew what to do, 'Almost in a way to say, I don't even want feedback.'
claims.passage: "Almost in a way to say, 'I don't even want feedback.'"
claims.inference: Alpert's account in Rolling Stone (S01): 'Stella came to us and said, I've unlocked something I've been looking for, and I know what to do. I can feel it', then, after the attribution, 'Almost in a way to say, I don't even want feedback.' The article paraphrases the first sentence and quotes the second. Billboard identifies him as chief executive of Disruptor Management (S17).
claims.alternative: Alpert was her manager and had every reason to tell a flattering story; Billboard later reported that she had left his company (C18), and the article says so two paragraphs on.

claims.claim: She says she wrote the 'Boston' chorus alone at a piano in Nashville shortly before a date and posted it; when commenters and then Noah Kahan's team noted its likeness to 'Stick Season', she said 'I want to do whatever accommodates him', and Kahan was credited.
claims.passage: "his team ended up reaching out and we had a conversation about it and I was just like, I want to do whatever accommodates him."
claims.inference: Direct quotation from The Line of Best Fit (S03). Edit stage: the article now labels this a concession with no later reversal, so it is not counted as an instance of the comply-then-reverse pattern. Her stated reason here is accommodation.
claims.alternative: Vanity Fair's writer says the credit prevented 'any risk of legal action' (C60), so prudence explains it as well as temperament does. Her statement that she was not thinking of Kahan is disputed (C61, C95); she answers that she is a fan who did not set out to borrow (C96).

claims.claim: Beyond the two credited interpolations, listeners and, in October 2026, two named artists have said other Lefty songs closely resemble earlier songs. No legal claim or finding has been reported, and she had not publicly addressed the comparisons as of October 11, 2026.
claims.passage: No legal claim or finding has been reported in the sources opened for this profile, and as of October 11, 2026, Lefty has not publicly addressed these comparisons.
claims.inference: What is established: Kahan is credited on 'Boston' (S17); the Chicks interpolation was cleared with Sony in June 2026 and the missing credit was blamed by the label on a streaming platform error, with documents reviewed by Rolling Stone (S22). What is alleged only: resemblances involving 'Why Wouldn't We', 'Misery', 'Seven Eleven' (S21) and the unreleased 'Badly', which Shaylen and TAELA compared to their song 'WATCH THIS' (S20). These are allegations and are not used here as evidence about her character or type.
claims.alternative: Melodic overlap is common in pop and country, interpolation is routine and often label-driven (S22), and no court, publisher or rights body has made a finding. The article does not use any of this as evidence of character or type, and the settle section now says her eventual answer will not be scored either.
claims.review_trigger: Any statement from Lefty, Atlantic Outpost, Shaylen, TAELA or the named songwriters; any credit change, takedown, settlement or lawsuit involving the listed songs; the release of 'Badly', with or without a credit. Recheck every named comparison at open_case.next_review (2026-12-01) and at each later refresh even if no news has been seen.

claims.claim: Since mid-2026 critics have called her a 'nepo baby' and an 'industry plant'. The narrow claim that the hit was manufactured is unsubstantiated (C65); how far family money financed her early career is unreported and unanswered (C100, C101).
claims.passage: critics have called her a "nepo baby" and an "industry plant,"
claims.inference: USA Today calls the manufactured-success claim 'unsubstantiated' and says the criticism 'centers on the significant advantages that enormous family wealth can provide, including time, training and the freedom to pursue a creative career' (S27). The New Yorker says the debate has turned to 'how lavishly he has financed her career' (S23). Edit stage: the article no longer says she concedes 'a different advantage'; time and a cushion are part of what the critics describe.
claims.alternative: Vanity Fair notes it is 'highly possible' her label paid for a social campaign, a tool it says any signed artist has (S02), and her then-manager Zach Horowitz told Billboard 'we've been building Stella's fan base for years' (S17). Neither is printed; both bear on how organic the rise was and should be weighed at the next refresh.
claims.review_trigger: New reporting on how her early career and marketing were financed, or a fuller first-person account from her or her father.

claims.claim: In August 2026 she replied to a fan who had resurfaced a 2022 clip of her swearing at Olivia Rodrigo: 'i was a stupid teenager posting random things on social media. i love olivia and never meant anything harmful by that.'
claims.passage: "i was a stupid teenager posting random things on social media. i love olivia and never meant anything harmful by that."
claims.inference: Holler quotes her TikTok comment (S18) and describes the clip as part of the Rodrigo and Sabrina Carpenter fan rivalry of the time. Edit stage: the article keeps this and the tour apology (C17) as the two short written replies and drops the SNL response.
claims.alternative: Read through an outlet's quotation; the original comment was not seen. Holler judges the clip 'clearly not meant to be taken seriously' (C102) and treats its resurfacing as part of an effort to discredit her. Two short posts in a managed autumn are thin evidence of temperament, as the article says.

claims.claim: After she stopped being an opening act on Tucker Wetmore's Brunette World Tour, with no announcement and no stated reason, she apologized around August 22-23, 2026: 'I wanted to announce that earlier but I was advised not to which was a mistake.'
claims.passage: "I wanted to announce that earlier but I was advised not to which was a mistake,"
claims.inference: Country Now quotes the post (S16). On her account she set aside her own inclination on advice and then called that a mistake. Edit stage: the article makes the reading conditional ('If she did want to announce it') and sets the rival reading beside it (C105), so the post is a possible brief instance of the pattern, not an established one.
claims.alternative: The wish is stated inside an apology, where a good prior intention is the expected thing to say, and naming the advice moves responsibility onto unnamed advisers. Who ended the opening slot, and why, is unknown. One episode, read through a secondary report.
claims.review_trigger: Any explanation of the withdrawal from Lefty, Wetmore or either team.

claims.claim: Billboard reported on September 27, 2026, citing unnamed sources, that she had left Disruptor Management (Adam Alpert and Zach Horowitz). No party commented.
claims.passage: Billboard's September 27 report, citing unnamed sources, said she had left Disruptor Management.
claims.inference: This is the first consequential break in her professional circle and it has no first-person account. How she eventually describes it is one of the few upcoming observations that could separate the type hypotheses (see open_case.settle_signals).
claims.alternative: Sourced anonymously and unconfirmed by either side. Reasons, and who initiated the split, are unknown; the article does not guess and no longer calls it her decision.
claims.review_trigger: Announcement of new management, or any on-record explanation from Lefty, Alpert or Horowitz.

claims.claim: Asked on Smooth Country, while promoting her single 'Good at Leaving', whether she is actually good at leaving, she said 'I was in the past for sure' because 'I used to be so afraid of love.'
claims.passage: "I used to be so afraid of love."
claims.inference: Caption and second transcription agree (S08). Edit stage: the article names the single, keeps her past tense, and drops 'habit', 'early' and 'leave-first history', which were the author's words. Her stated reason is fear, which is why the answer is listed as shared between Seven and Six.
claims.alternative: The question plays on the title of the song being promoted, so the answer doubles as song talk. Wariness after a breakup at 22 or 23 is ordinary. She says the pattern has ended.

claims.claim: Her stated aim for the music is a song that makes her feel happy in the car.
claims.passage: music that makes her feel happy in the car
claims.inference: Paraphrase of B96, August 7, 2026 (S14): 'I just want to be able to get into my car and listen to whatever song that I'm making and make me feel happy... That's the goal for me.' Edit stage: the Seven case now rests on option-keeping (C44) more than on mood words.
claims.alternative: It is also brand positioning: upbeat, easy country-pop is the product she is selling in every one of these interviews. The article says so in the same sentence.

claims.claim: A reporter who followed her through three CMA Fest appearances in under two hours in June 2026 observed that everyone around her seemed panicked about time 'except for Lefty herself', and that her reaction to a capacity crowd was that she needed to go home and write more songs.
claims.passage: "Everyone seems a little panicked that we won't make it where we need to go in time, except for Lefty herself."
claims.inference: This is the only extended third-party observation of her under time pressure. It shows composure while her team is agitated and a turn back to routine work after a peak moment.
claims.alternative: One afternoon, one reporter, a managed setting with her parents present, in a sympathetic feature. Keeping to the schedule is her handlers' job, not hers, which the article now says. In the same scene she tells the reporter 'I'm a little worried about my voice' (S01).

claims.claim: She says that two years before her breakthrough it was more stressful than touring because 'I wanted it all so badly.'
claims.passage: "I wanted it all so badly."
claims.inference: Caption and second transcription agree (S08). Her own words establish strong appetite before the success. It is evidence against a low-drive reading and for the Type 3 and Type 7 alternatives; the article lists it under Type 3.
claims.alternative: Said lightly, as advice to her younger self to 'chill'. Wanting a career badly at 22 is not type-specific.

claims.claim: She has voiced worry about whether she belongs in country music as a Midwesterner ('I'm not Southern. I always worried, Do I have to be?').

claims.claim: Outside critics hear her country turn as adopted. The New Yorker's Brady Brickner-Wood wrote on August 5, 2026 that 'in her singing she's adopted a raspy Southern twang.'

Edit stage: the checkable evidence on her side (C91, C92) now sits beside it. The same essay calls her 'yet another competent, country-curious folk-pop artist chasing the success of' a current crossover hit, which is not printed.
claims.alternative: Reviews assess records and delivery, not motives, and some carry errors (The Guardian calls her 'Cali-raised', S24). She says country was the music she grew up on (S02, S03).

claims.claim: As of October 11, 2026, the people quoted describing her firsthand are collaborators, her then-managers, tourmates and the singer Vincent Mason, whom 2026 coverage calls her boyfriend.

Rolling Stone calls Mason her boyfriend (June 2026) and Vanity Fair 'her now boyfriend' (August 2026); Alpert, Horowitz, Kasher, Enger, Flores and Smyers are managers, collaborators or acts she has performed with. The sentence is dated and says 'that year', so it asserts no current relationship or current management.
claims.alternative: Kelsea Ballerini, Randy Travis and Tia Sillers are quoted in support of her or about a song, not describing her from contact. Her mother is paraphrased, not quoted.
claims.review_trigger: Any change in the relationship or in her management, and any on-record testimony from someone who knew her before 2024.

claims.inference: Same answer as C07 in The Line of Best Fit; several sentences separate the two quoted lines, so the article prints them as separate statements. The answer continues 'That really had me spiraling' (C106).

claims.inference: 'I like pivoted for a whole year and was making more like pop' (S13); 'that's what they all wanted me to do' (S05); 'There were so many people telling me that I had to really stay away from country' (S02). Edit stage correction: the adviser framing is now attributed to her later tellings, because her earliest telling (S13) names no adviser. The H2, the description and the FAQs no longer state it as fact.

claims.review_trigger: Any long-form interview given after September 27, 2026, or any pre-2026 interview that surfaces.

claims.claim: The 60-word type answer: leading read Type 9 at low confidence, Type 6 the closest rival, Types 7 and 3 live; she describes going along and reversing later once at length (Los Angeles) and once briefly (the tour announcement), and her stated reasons fit more than one type.
claims.passage: Leading read: Type 9, held loosely, at low confidence.
claims.inference: Summarizes type_hypothesis. The same text is the first FAQ answer. Edit stage: 'repeatedly' is gone and the count is the same in the answer, the pattern paragraph and the closing paragraph; the span is given as March to August 2026 in place of 'seven-month'.

claims.review_trigger: Any of the open_case.settle_signals; reopen on open_case.next_review (2026-12-01). If that review finds no settle signal, move next_review to a date after February 20, 2027.

claims.claim: Rolling Stone's writer says she turned the Nashville publishing deal down.

Edit stage: 'turned the deal down' is now attributed to the writer.

Second transcription: 'So I was like, oh, this is too country. I was afraid.' Both transcriptions agree on the two printed fragments. Edit stage: 'I was afraid' was checked against both before printing, as the Enneagram review asked; it refers to holding the country song back. Fear is one of her stated reasons for the pop year.
claims.alternative: How long she held it varies by telling ('a few months' in S05, 'like 6 months' in S13); the article gives no duration. No human has listened to the audio.

claims.alternative: 'Right after Christmas' and 'December' agree; the article now presents them as one dating.

claims.claim: She says she refuses suggestions to pick a single genre lane.

claims.alternative: Also a commercially sound crossover position. Billboard's quote ('Every time we've been talking about doing something') does not say who made the suggestion.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the pattern the profile counts runs one way, comply first and reverse later. The Los Angeles year fits it at length; the August 2026 tour announcement may fit it briefly; the Kahan credit is a concession with no reversal; the publisher episode is the mirror image.

claims.inference: Edit stage rewrite. The frozen draft summed the publisher and Los Angeles episodes as 'one sequence' appearing 'twice' although they run in opposite directions. The pattern is now defined in one direction and each episode is labeled once. The same count (once at length, once briefly) appears in the type answer, the first FAQ and the closing paragraph.
claims.alternative: The long instance is one episode retold across interviews with varying accounts (C10); the brief one is a single post read through an outlet (C17). The pattern fits Six as well as Nine (C110).

claims.claim: She says 'Thinking 'bout You' was her most viral video, 'at the top of this year', after the December decision.

claims.alternative: By her account the decision came first (C42), but the two are weeks apart at most and both were told afterward (C109).

claims.inference: Wording follows the YouTube caption track. A second machine transcription matched except for one word, which it garbled ('sweating for music'); the caption reading 'profusely' is kept.

claims.claim: When friends objected that she was writing songs about boys they knew, she says her answer was 'well it's the truth so.'
claims.passage: "well it's the truth so."
claims.inference: Caption and second transcription agree. She adds that some friends had befriended the ex she was writing about.
claims.alternative: Her own retelling years later. Persisting despite friends' objections cuts against a conflict-avoidant reading, as the draft says.

claims.claim: She posted two takes of the unfinished 'Boston' chorus, one smiling and one less so, on a secondary account for material she is unsure about, guessing the smiling one would do better; it did.
claims.passage: on a side account "where I post things that I'm like not so sure about," guessing that "the smiling one will do better."
claims.inference: Caption and second transcription agree on both quoted fragments ('my like covers account, which is where I post things that I'm like not so sure about'; 'maybe like the smiling one will do better and it did'). Z100 (S10) also mentions the covers account.
claims.alternative: Which motive the testing serves (winning the audience, checking safe ground, or a generational working method) is not settled by the record.

claims.claim: She told Vanity Fair, 'Nobody has the answer anymore for how to make something work. TikTok decides.'
claims.passage: "Nobody has the answer anymore for how to make something work. TikTok decides,"
claims.inference: Direct quotation from Vanity Fair (S02), now printed in full. The same sentence carries the profile's report that she and her co-writers say they do not think about the algorithm while writing (C94).
claims.alternative: Vanity Fair calls daily testing a requirement for anyone trying to make it in music today.

claims.claim: Unexplained: why one listener is harder for her than thousands when she sang to a phone almost daily and, per Rolling Stone, played in-person gigs as half of a duo.
claims.passage: She says one listener is harder than thousands, yet she sang to a phone almost daily and, by Rolling Stone's account, to rooms as half of a duo.
claims.inference: Edit stage rewrite. The frozen sentence said a room frightened her for years while a phone did not, which ran past Rolling Stone's report of live gigs (C93). The contradiction is kept open with accurate scope, and 'says only' is narrowed to 'Nothing firmly attributable to her explains why.'
claims.alternative: The next line in the Snapchat video ('With one person, you're like, oh my god, do you hate me?') cannot be assigned to her or the host from captions and is not used; resolving the speaker is an open research task. She has also described coping in different ways (deciding one day, nerves as adrenaline, asking Marcus Mumford whether he still gets nervous, S08; tequila, S07), none of which is printed.

claims.claim: Noah Kahan is credited as a writer on 'Boston.'
claims.passage: Kahan is credited as a writer on the song, according to Billboard
claims.inference: Billboard, May 13, 2026: 'Stick Season writer Kahan is credited on Boston'; repeated on September 27, 2026. The article glosses interpolation as reworking part of an existing melody, following Rolling Stone's definition (S22).

claims.claim: Vanity Fair's writer states that the credit was given before the song officially came out, 'preventing any risk of legal action.'
claims.passage: "before the song officially came out, preventing any risk of legal action."
claims.inference: The phrase is the writer's, and the draft attributes it to the writer.
claims.alternative: Paste's 'impending lawsuit' wording (S33) goes beyond anything the interviews report and is not used.

claims.passage: "When I was writing the song, I wasn't thinking about Noah Kahan"
claims.inference: Her statement is from Vanity Fair (S02). Edit stage: the doubt is attributed to named reporting (C95), her on-record position is printed beside it (C96), and the scope of the missing videos is given in C81.

claims.review_trigger: Any further statement from Lefty or Kahan about the song.

claims.passage: "Summer You Were Mine" interpolates the Chicks' "There's Your Trouble,"
claims.inference: The one similarity dispute with documentary evidence reviewed by a reporter (S22). Edit stage: the sentence saying the writers 'are now listed' was cut, so no undated present-tense credit status remains in the body.

claims.passage: fans had compared "Why Wouldn't We," "Seven Eleven" and "Misery" to earlier songs by other artists, and none credited those writers
claims.inference: Reported as fan allegations by Rolling Stone's explainer (S21), which names the earlier songs (by Blake Shelton and Wheatus, and one from The Greatest Showman) and says their writers are not credited. Edit stage: the credit status now carries the explainer's date, and the earlier songs' names were cut for length. Not used as evidence of character or type.

claims.review_trigger: Any credit change, statement, takedown, settlement or lawsuit involving these songs. Recheck each song's credits at open_case.next_review (2026-12-01) and at each later refresh.

claims.alternative: The outlet is opinionated and hostile to her music; its characterizations are its own. TAELA also wrote 'we will not tear another woman down but we will stand up for something we created', which is not printed. No claim, credit change or response had been reported.

claims.review_trigger: New reporting on how her early career and marketing were financed.

claims.claim: She told Vanity Fair that her upbringing gave her time and a cushion.

claims.alternative: Time is part of what her critics describe, not a different advantage (C14). The same concession Gracie Abrams has made, as Vanity Fair notes.

Edit stage: 'decisions' became 'changes', the unnamed-sources and unconfirmed attribution travels with every mention, and the sentence carries an as-of date.

claims.review_trigger: Any on-record explanation from Lefty, Wetmore, Alpert or Horowitz, or a correction to the Billboard report.

claims.claim: Rolling Stone reports that her plan after graduation had been Nashville and that the producer J Kash and her managers at Disruptor urged her to move to Los Angeles.
claims.passage: her plan had been Nashville and that the producer J Kash and her managers at Disruptor urged the move to Los Angeles
claims.inference: 'After graduation, she had plans to move to Nashville' and 'Both J Kash and her new management team at Disruptor Records urged her to move to Los Angeles' (S01). Vanity Fair says Kasher 'convinced her to move to LA instead of Nashville' (S02).

claims.inference: Caption: 'then I like pivoted for a whole year and was making more like pop pop'. Second transcription: 'And then I pivoted for a whole year'. The printed fragment is common to both.

It is a third stated reason for the pop year, and the one the Type 3 paragraph argues from.

claims.claim: Vanity Fair says the publishing deal 'fell through'.
claims.passage: Vanity Fair says it "fell through."
claims.inference: 'Midway through college, Pulse Music Group offered her a publishing deal writing for other artists. When the deal fell through, she decided maybe she wanted to be a singer after all' (S02).

claims.passage: In The Line of Best Fit, the publisher declined to sign her.

claims.passage: In her quoted tellings she resists at once, perhaps only in thought, and agrees months later.

claims.passage: The low views are both the cost she names and the plainest commercial reason for what came next.
claims.inference: Her quotation (C40) and Vanity Fair's framing ('her pop experiments were not successful. The proof was in the like count', S02); on MuchMusic she says that in Los Angeles 'nothing was working. Like truly, videos would get like a thousand views max' (S07, both transcriptions agree).
claims.alternative: She presents the turn as taste first and response second; the record cannot separate them (C109).

claims.claim: Rolling Stone describes college-era posts covering Tyler Childers and the Band Perry and a 2024 debut single, 'Kiss Me', which it says went viral, all before the 2025 pop EP.
claims.passage: Rolling Stone describes college-era covers of Tyler Childers and the Band Perry and a viral 2024 debut single, "Kiss Me," before the pop EP
claims.inference: 'Sometimes, it was those covers, of Childers, the Band Perry, and Noah Kahan's Stick Season', 'her 2024 debut single, Kiss Me' and 'Her first original, Kiss Me, went viral' (S01). She calls 'Kiss Me' a viral song from when she was starting out (S05); Whiskey Riff dates the single to November 2024 (S20). This is the checkable support for a country lean that predates the pop year, and the main point against reading the country turn as adopted.
claims.alternative: The article does not characterize 'Kiss Me' musically; her description of her first release as a pop-country blend (S13) is hers alone and is not printed. The old posts are no longer public (C81).

claims.claim: She told The Line of Best Fit that country radio in her father's car was her first introduction to music.
claims.passage: she told The Line of Best Fit that country radio in her father's car came first
claims.inference: 'My dad in particular was the first intro to music that I ever had because country radio was blasting in the car no matter where we were going' (S03). She says the same to Vanity Fair and Billboard.
claims.alternative: A retrospective account that also answers the authenticity charge.

claims.claim: Rolling Stone reports that in the years she was posting herself singing she 'played some real, in-person gigs, often as a duo called Stella + Huck.'
claims.passage: "played some real, in-person gigs, often as a duo called Stella + Huck."
claims.inference: The writer's sentence, in the feature's account of the years after she began posting her singing in 2022 (S01). Added at the edit stage: it is the main correction to the frozen draft's 'hidden' framing and to the room-versus-phone puzzle.

type_hypothesis.against: (1) Drive. She 'wanted it all so badly' (C27), says she could post '700 times a day' (C08), sang whatever cover was going viral (C09) and tested takes for response (C55). That is more appetite than the easygoing Nine picture allows, and her reply to a capacity crowd was that she needed to write more songs (C70). (2) She kept posting songs about boys her friends knew over their objections (C51), and by her own account her first reaction to the publisher was anger, not accommodation (C07, C89). (3) Lifelong stage fright (C05, C48), 'really had me spiraling' (C106) and 'I was afraid' (C41) read as anxiety more than calm. (4) Nearly every accommodating act has a practical explanation: the Kahan credit avoided legal risk (C60), following managers at 22 is ordinary (C10), and not fighting critics is standard media advice (C16). (5) The long instance of the pattern is one episode retold three different ways (C10), and the brief one is a single post whose stated intention sits inside an apology (C105). (6) The whole first-person record was produced inside one promotional campaign, where agreeable and upbeat is the expected register (C36).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 6 is the closest rival, changed from Type 7 at the edit stage on the Enneagram reviewer's finding (enneagram-02); the leading type is unchanged. The comply-then-reverse pattern fits Six as well as Nine, since a Six also defers to advisers and later regrets it. Her own stated reasons for the pop year are belonging and fear: 'because I wasn't from the South', 'it really got in my head' (C10), 'I was afraid' (C41), 'I always worried, Do I have to be?' (C28). She describes lifelong stage fright (C05), says the publisher's verdict 'really had me spiraling' (C106), tests uncertain songs on a side account (C55), names the advice when it went wrong (C17) and explained herself when 'Boston' was challenged (C75). Unprinted but in the record: she asked Marcus Mumford whether he still gets nervous (S08) and told a reporter 'I'm a little worried about my voice' (S01). Against Six there is nothing firm. The frozen draft's counter, that she questions or justifies herself little under attack, was withdrawn because her quoted statements contradict it. Nine leads only on the ease of her concessions (C12) and one reporter's observation of composure (C23), both with ordinary explanations (C110). Type 7 is live and unranked: fun and happiness are her stated aim (C21), though that is also the product's pitch; she refuses to pick a lane (C44); and she says she was good at leaving in the past, for a fear reason that Six claims equally (C19, C107). What strains Seven is that, if her later tellings are accurate, she stayed a year in a direction she did not want (C108). Type 3 is live and unranked, and is the read closest to what her critics say: she sang what was going viral (C09), tested takes (C55), says 'TikTok decides' (C56), 'wanted it all so badly' (C27) and entered the pop year partly for what she thought success required (C86); both turns fit 'whatever is working' (C112). Against Three: she places the decision before the viral response, weeks apart and told afterward (C109), and country covers predate the pop year (C91). The record does not rank Seven and Three.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: None that is defensible yet. The best candidate is what she does when someone else's direction collides with her own preference, defined in one direction: comply first, reverse later (C45). One long episode fits it, the Los Angeles year (C10), and one brief one may, the August 2026 tour announcement (C17, C105). The Kahan credit is a concession with no reversal (C12), and the publisher episode runs the other way (C89). That sequence fits Nine better than a Seven who felt boxed in (C108) and is weak against Three, because her reversal has never been observed against a direction that was working (C109). It does not separate Nine from Six at all (C110). Every instance is her own retelling during a press cycle, the tellings of the long instance differ, and the rival reading, that disappointments get attributed to other people's advice, fits the same statements. On this record the leading read cannot be held above low confidence, so the profile is an open case.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Why one listener is harder for her than thousands when she sang to a phone almost daily and played in-person gigs (C57). Whether the pop-to-country turn was a recovery of her own taste or a move toward the audience that responded; her account and the numbers point the same way (C90, C109). Whether anyone in particular told her to avoid country, and who. Why her opening slot on the Wetmore tour ended and why she and Disruptor Management reportedly parted, and who made either call (C82). How far family money financed her early career (C101). Why her posts from before August 2025 are no longer public (C81). How she behaves in a direct conflict with someone close to her: no one has described one.

open_case.reason: Stella Lefty is 24 and less than a year into public life: her first viral single came in January 2026, 'Boston' was released on March 27, 2026 and her debut album on August 21, 2026. Every interview in the record dates from March 27 to August 21, 2026 and belongs to one promotional campaign, mostly 5-to-20-minute radio and festival spots plus two magazine profiles, in which the same handful of stories recurs, not always the same way. The only people quoted describing her from personal contact are collaborators, her then-managers, tourmates and her boyfriend as of 2026. Her TikTok archive from before August 2025 is no longer public. Two consequential changes in her first year (the end of her opening slot on a tour, and a management split reported by Billboard from unnamed sources) have no first-person account, and no source says who made either call. Thirty-three sources were opened and four types tested. The leading read (Nine) and its closest rival (Six) are not separated by anything in the record, and Seven and Three remain live; the hypotheses disagree mainly about what her going along and her drive are for.
settle_signals: Her own unscripted, long-form account of going along, in Los Angeles or over the August 2026 tour announcement: does she describe not registering what she wanted, or not thinking it worth the friction (Nine), or doubting her own judgment and wanting backing (Six)? After the reported management change, does she settle into her own course (Nine) or stay watchful about whom to trust (Six)? Her existing statement, 'I was advised not to which was a mistake', fits both. A prepared statement does not count, and an explanation that is logistical, medical, contractual or not hers to give settles nothing about type.

The first release where her taste and the numbers pull apart: does she follow the numbers (Three), keep to what she likes at a cost (points away from Three), or move quickly to something new (Seven)? Following advisers cannot separate Six from Nine. Her account of the 2025 EP's low views is the baseline, and it does not count as this test because the pop year had already failed when she reversed.

The first on-record testimony from someone who knew her before 2024 (a sibling, college friend, teacher or the other half of Stella + Huck) describing her in a disagreement: going quiet and smoothing it over would favor Nine; pressing the point and then checking where she stands would favor Six. This signal says less about Seven or Three.
